title: RNase E resolves toxic condensates by counteracting phase separation of Type II RhlB helicases.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full supplementary bundle. The only machine-readable data file is 'Table S3.xlsx' (211 KB, 3 sheets): I parsed it and counted 298 data rows = 149 unique pepsin peptides measured in exactly 2 protein states (RhlB alone, RhlB + RNase E) at 3 timepoints (3 s, 30 s, 300 s), reported as number of deuterons (#D) and percent deuteration (%D) with standard deviations and replicate counts. I also listed all 25 pages of captions in the supplementary PDF: Tables S1 (peptide list from liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry), S2 (hydrogen-deuterium exchange experimental details), S4-S6 (strains, plasmids, primers), and Figures S1-S11 (phylogenetic tree, alignments, gels, microscopy).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The data availability statement ('available in the article and in its online supplementary material'), the absence of any repository accession (Europe PMC reports no cross-references and no text-mined accessions; no Protein Data Bank, ProteomeXchange or sequencing deposition exists), and the biological conclusions about phase separation, growth at low temperature and RNase E binding, all of which rest on images of gels, microscopy and growth curves rather than on tabular data.

a1_downloadable.note: Supplementary zip (2.7 MB) downloads openly from Europe PMC with no login; I extracted it. No repository accession exists, so the supplement is all there is.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. There is no prediction target anywhere in the files. The one data table holds deuterium uptake for 149 peptides of a single protein; every biological outcome in the paper (does this helicase form droplets, does RNase E dissolve them, does the strain grow at 16 degrees C) exists only as microscopy and gel images, so any label would have to be constructed by hand from figures.

a3_inputs_present.note: Peptide amino-acid sequences with start/end residue numbers are present as columns in Table S3a; no accession lookups needed. Checked in the file.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit in the sheet headers: number of deuterons (#D), percent deuteration (%D), timepoints in seconds, standard deviation columns. Checked in the file.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. 298 rows total = 149 unique peptides x 2 states, one protein, one organism. The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows (~400 for classification). Counted directly in Table S3.xlsx.

a6_fits_laptop.note: The entire usable dataset is a 211 KB spreadsheet; trivially fits. Verified by opening it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper points to Table S2 for replicate counts and Table S3 for raw data; the replicate columns in S3a (3/3/2 and 3/3/3 per state) match the states described in the text. No count conflict found.

a8_label_provenance.note: The deuterium uptake values are a direct physical measurement by mass spectrometry, not a model output. Provenance is fine; there simply is no label to predict.

honest_claim_h3: No honest machine-learning claim is available from this paper's data: with 149 peptides from one protein in two conditions, any model would describe a single experiment rather than a generalisable relationship.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use bacterial helicase protein sequence to predict whether it forms liquid droplets and how deuterium exchange changes on partner binding.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on the paper's hydrogen-deuterium exchange table (a mass-spectrometry readout of how exposed each short stretch of a protein is to solvent): 149 peptide stretches of one Pseudomonas aeruginosa RhlB helicase, each measured in 2 conditions. That is the verified count, and it is the entire machine-readable dataset.
plain_idea.predict: Either per-peptide deuterium uptake change on binding of the partner enzyme RNase E, or a protein-level yes/no for droplet formation (liquid-liquid phase separation). The true answer comes from mass spectrometry for the former and from fluorescence microscopy images, not tabulated, for the latter.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Bacterial condensate biology is genuinely under-modelled compared with human proteins, so a sequence-to-droplet model for bacteria would interest microbiologists studying RNA degradosomes; but this paper supplies one protein, not a training set.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: predict per-peptide deuterium uptake change (a protein-dynamics readout) or droplet-forming propensity from sequence. The paper is a single-protein mechanistic study; its only table is 149 peptides of one helicase in two states, and the phase-separation and growth phenotypes exist solely as microscopy and gel images. A viable version of this idea would have to be built from a public phase-separation resource (for example LLPSDB or PhaSepDB) plus bacterial proteome sequences, with this paper contributing at most one or two validation examples.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the actual file: a 211 KB spreadsheet parsed in under a second with pandas. Compute is a non-issue; the dataset is simply too small to model.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in Table S3.xlsx and the number of distinct proteins in it. Answer: 298 rows, 1 protein, 2 states. That killed it in five minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails A2 and A5: no prediction-target column anywhere in the files, and the single data table holds only 298 rows (149 peptides, one protein, two conditions) of hydrogen-deuterium exchange. Every phenotype the paper is actually about - droplet formation, growth at low temperature, binding interfaces - is recorded as microscopy and gel images, so a label would have to be built by hand from figures. Verified by downloading and parsing the supplement; this is a well-executed mechanistic biochemistry paper with no machine-learning dataset attached.
